flag_detail: Land seizure/displacement (Villa Ukika, the Yagán settlement, adjoins the Navy town; relocation mechanics not confirmed); rescue results 'pendiente'

name: Sistema de fuertes de Valdivia (Mancera, Corral, Niebla, Amargos)
beneath: Huilliche territory. Test pits by Rodrigo Mera, Leonor Adan, Simon Urbina and others (Fondart project, 5-9 Nov 2007) in the Casa del Castellano and beside the church inside Castillo San Pedro de Alcantara on Isla Mancera reached cultural deposits to c.1.5 m with 'restos culturales prehispanicos' on the same terrace on which the castle was built: Vergel and Valdivia-phase ceramics and possibly Pitren pottery beneath colonial and republican layers. No pre-Hispanic deposit is published for Niebla, Corral or Amargos

name: Fuerte Bulnes (Punta Santa Ana)
beneath: Punta Santa Ana holds a sequence of marine hunter-gatherer (canoe-people, ancestral Kawesqar) shell-midden sites: PSA-1 (c. 6300 BP, Ortiz-Troncoso), PSA-2 (c. 2700 BP) and PSA-3 (c. 700-1000 BP), with PSA-3's upper layers disturbed by the mid-20th-century reconstruction of Fuerte Bulnes and vehicle traffic (Morello et al., Magallania 40(2), 2012)
flag_detail: Destroyed (partial: the 1940s reconstruction of the fort and vehicle traffic removed and mixed the surface layers of the PSA-3 shell midden - Morello et al. 2012)

name: Fuerte Sancti Spiritu (Puerto Gaboto)
beneath: A stable Indigenous settlement on the Carcarañá: per Azkarate the Spanish settled on the settlement, 'partly occupied and destroyed to build the fort'; excavations from 2006 located the site
relationship: Built directly on a known site
flag_detail: Destroyed (1527: part of the settlement razed for the fort)

name: Fuerte del Carmen / Cerro de la Caballada (Carmen de Patagones)
beneath: Jan 2022 trenching exposed human remains: 17 individuals with lithic artifacts; two burials dated 1700 and 1800 BP
relationship_note: burials confirmed on the historic site; fort structures probable
flag_detail: Destroyed (burials disturbed by machinery in 2022, then rescued)

name: Fuerte Ushuaia / Base Naval Ushuaia
beneath: Yámana (Yagán) territory (>11,000 years on Tierra del Fuego); the Navy post was placed on the site of the Anglican mission where Yagán had been gathered; no pre-Hispanic site beneath documented

name: Campo de Mayo
beneath: No Querandí or other pre-Hispanic site documented
flag_detail: None documented (1976–83 detention centres not examined)

name: Conquest-of-the-Desert fortines (Pescado, Machado, Tapera de Sabino; cf. Otamendi, General Paz, Blanca Grande)
beneath: Bagaloni & Martí (2021): no Indigenous occupation layers beneath or mixed with the fortlets studied; some roads followed Indigenous trails
flag_detail: Land seizure (the frontier advance 'culminated in the early 1880s')

name: Fortaleza de Santa Teresa (Parque Nacional Santa Teresa)
builder: Portugal 1762; Spain; Uruguayan Army (runs the park)
beneath: No cerrito de indios inside the fortress parcel; large mound-builder cerrito concentrations 'a escasos km' (Potrero Grande, San Miguel marshes)

name: Fuerte de San Miguel (Rocha)
beneath: Cerrito concentrations in the San Miguel marshes; none documented under the fort

name: Casa Fuerte de Nuestra Señora de la Asunción
beneath: Founded in Cario-Guaraní territory with whom the Spanish allied; no excavation of a Cario village under the fort found

name: Fuerte Borbón / Fuerte Olimpo (Alto Paraguay)
beneath: Mbayá caciques invited to the founding; Chamacoco/Ishir lands; no site beneath documented
flag_detail: Land seizure (post-1870 latifundia used 'mano de obra indígena en la práctica esclavizada')

name: Chaco War fortines (Isla Po'i, Pilcomayo fortines, Ingavi, Boquerón)
beneath: Bolivia placed most fortines near Nivaclé villages; Isla Po'i 'was built in the middle of Enlhet territory'; Ingavi in Ayoreo territory — living Indigenous villages of the early 20th century, not archaeological sites
relationship: Deliberate reuse of an Indigenous place
flag_detail: Land seizure/displacement and Destroyed (massacres; an aerial bombing wiped out a Nivaclé village; Enlhet forced to guide, build roads and dig trenches; after 1935 the Nivaclé were disarmed and ranchers took their land)

name: Forte Marechal Luz (São Francisco do Sul)
builder: Portugal (18th-c. battery); Brazilian Army coastal fort 1909–15
beneath: The Sambaqui do Forte Marechal Luz: a shell mound with a pre-ceramic burial layer and later ceramic layer excavated by Alan Bryan in the 1960s (32 individuals analysed); exact relation to the ramparts not stated
relationship: Built directly on a known site
flag_detail: Access Army-mediated (fee; group visits via the unit); no destruction documented

name: Centro de Lançamento de Alcântara (CLA)
builder: Brazilian Air Force (expropriation decree 12 Sept 1980; activated 1 Mar 1983)
beneath: IPHAN records the Tupinambá village cluster Tapuitapera in the Alcântara area from 1612; no inventory of pre-colonial sites inside the CLA found
relationship_note: historic Tupinambá territory; specific sites unverified
flags: Land seizure / displacement; Litigation / inquiry; Restricted access
flag_detail: Land seizure/displacement and Litigation (documented — colonial-era quilombola communities, not pre-Columbian): 312 families from 31 settlements moved to agrovilas with no sea access, mainly Jul–Dec 1986 and Nov 1987–Dec 1988 (expropriation by State Decree 7,820 of 12 Sep 1980; CLA created by Federal Decree 88,136 of 1 Mar 1983); IACHR petition 17 Aug 2001, admissibility report 83/06 (2006), merits report 189/20 (2020); Inter-American Court judgment 21 Nov 2024 ordered collective title to 78,105 ha within three years, good-faith consultation and a public act of recognition; Restricted access (launch-window and fishing restrictions on the agrovilas)

name: Base Aérea do Galeão / Estação Rádio da Marinha (Ilha do Governador)
beneath: Tupi Paranapuã island (Temiminó in 1502); the Aldeia Tupi da Estação Rádio da Marinha is an 18th-century Tupi village site on the Navy radio-station grounds; no sambaqui under the air base documented
relationship_note: post-contact village (18th c.); air base unverified
flag_detail: Destroyed (an inlet filled for runway 10/28; Guanabara sambaquis 'obliterados' by urban growth — no site named)

name: Forte do Presépio / Forte do Castelo (Belém)
beneath: Built 'na ponta de Mairi', the Indigenous-named point at the Guamá mouth; attacked by Tupinambá under Guaimiaba (killed 1619); a village directly beneath unverified
flag_detail: Destroyed and Land seizure (enslavement of the region's Indigenous people; 1619–20 reprisals that decimated the Tapajós village)

name: Forte de Coimbra (Corumbá)
beneath: Pre-colonial rock-art/burial caves inside the fort area (Gruta do Inferno) not mentioned in the source opened

name: Fortalezas of Santa Catarina island (Anhatomirim; São José da Ponta Grossa)
beneath: Carijó-Guaraní island; no sambaqui or pre-colonial layer under either fort documented (1987–92 archaeology was historical)

name: Forte dos Reis Magos (Natal)
beneath: Potiguar territory; built on a tidal reef — no pre-colonial site beneath

name: Centre Spatial Guyanais (Kourou–Sinnamary)
beneath: Inrap excavation Eva 2 (2006): an Archaic occupation c. 4500–2000 BC in a palaeosol, ceramics from c. 2200 BC; 'la carrière dite Eva' was quarried by the CSG for the Soyuz launch pad; Luna diagnostic (2015) for Ariane 6 found Archaic and historic Amerindian occupations
relationship: Built directly on a known site
relationship_note: civil space centre, not a military installation
flag_detail: Destroyed (hilltop quarried for the Soyuz pad, mitigated by excavation; the Archaic layer was missed at diagnostic stage); finds previewed to Amerindian customary chiefs 11 Aug 2019

name: Fort Zeelandia (Paramaribo)
beneath: The Indigenous village Parmurbo is widely cited but not mentioned in the source opened
relationship: Deliberate reuse of an Indigenous place
flag_detail: None documented (pre-Columbian); 1982 December murders are post-contact

name: Fort Kyk-Over-Al (Essequibo)
beneath: No prior Indigenous settlement on the island documented

name: Atkinson Field / Timehri (Cheddi Jagan International Airport; Base Camp Stephenson adjoins)
beneath: Timehri means rock drawings, but no petroglyph or pre-colonial site on the airfield is documented
flag_detail: Destroyed (hills levelled in 1941; no site named)

name: Cartagena de Indias (walled city; Castillo San Felipe de Barajas; Base Naval ARC Bolívar)
beneath: Heredia founded the city 'in the former seat of the indigenous Caribbean Calamarí village'; subsidiary groups at Pie de la Popa below the San Felipe hill; naval base unverified
relationship: Deliberate reuse of an Indigenous place
relationship_note: city on Calamarí Confirmed; naval base Unverified
flag_detail: None documented in sources opened (fate of the Calamarí not described)

name: Santa Marta (Spanish city and forts El Morro, San Fernando; Base Naval)
beneath: Matuna lands: the conquistadors 'expulsaron a los matunas' and razed other peoples' settlements; Tairona war 1501–1600; naval base unverified
flag_detail: Land seizure/displacement and Destroyed (16th-century expulsion; 1600: >70 caciques executed, survivors displaced)

name: Tumaco — Base Naval del Pacífico
beneath: The El Morro site, on Isla El Morro at the entrance to Tumaco bay where the naval complex stands: a 1996 excavation by J.-F. Bouchard (CNRS) 'en los terrenos del Centro de Control de Contaminacion del Pacifico' (CCCP, a DIMAR/Armada Nacional facility) found a Tumaco-La Tolita occupation followed by a 'Morro' phase midden dated c. 350-450 CE; 1978 trenches were dug in the Capitania de Puerto. Bouchard notes no pre-Hispanic remains have been found on the other Tumaco islands, so the earlier 'island-wide' reading is narrowed to El Morro
flag_detail: Destroyed (partial: Bouchard records the site damaged by construction of the port warehouses and pier in 1949-50 and by post-1979-tsunami settlement on its southern part; artificial mounds on the mainland lost to brickworks and shrimp ponds)

name: Castillo de San Antonio de la Eminencia (Cumaná)
beneath: No pre-Hispanic occupation of the hill documented

name: Castillo de San Carlos de la Barra (Zulia)
beneath: Añú palafito lakeshore; no site beneath documented

name: Tiwanaku — military damage allegation (no installation)
beneath: Tiwanaku ceremonial core: damage attributed (uncited) to stone quarrying for railways and 'target practice by military personnel'
flag_detail: Destroyed (allegation: target practice; uncited in the source)

name: Cuartel Real de Lima / Centro Cultural Metropolitano (Quito)
beneath: No Inca remains under the building documented

name: Pumapungo (Cuenca)
beneath: Inca military fort on a Cañari site; destroyed in the Inca civil war; no colonial or national cuartel use found

name: Campamento militar de Toniná (Mexican Army camp at the Toniná ruins, Ocosingo)
builder: Mexican Army (SEDENA), established during the post-1994 militarisation of the Zapatista conflict zone
beneath: Toniná, the Classic Maya acropolis-city of Ocosingo (Popol/Toniná dynasty, AD c.300–900). A June 1996 international civil observer delegation report (LAI/Otros Mundos Chiapas) recorded: "Hay un campamento militar en las ruinas de Toniná, rancho Majosil y Nuevo Jerusalén, con 2 mil soldados", with armoured vehicles, helicopters and light tanks. No INAH report on physical impact located.
relationship: Deliberate reuse of an Indigenous place
relationship_note: camp placed at the ruins; extent of overlap with the monumental core not documented
flag_detail: Alleged: occupation of an INAH-protected Maya site by a 2,000-strong army camp during counter-insurgency deployment (1996 observer report). No destruction, repatriation or litigation documented; not corroborated by INAH or HRW sources opened.

name: BDF Conservation Post at Caracol (Belize Defence Force Caracol camp, Chiquibul)
location: Caracol Archaeological Reserve, Cayo District, Belize (near the Guatemalan border)
builder: Government of Belize / Belize Defence Force with the Institute of Archaeology (NICH); inaugurated July 2015
beneath: Caracol, the largest Classic Maya city in Belize (c.600 BC–AD 900, with over 25,000 structures across c.177 km2). The permanent BDF post, housing twelve soldiers with quarters, showers and radio, was placed inside the Caracol Archaeological Reserve near the site core so that soldiers can patrol the epicentre and surroundings after the 2014 killing of a tourism police officer at the ruins; it is linked to the Douglas D Silva and Belizario Camp bases.
relationship: Deliberate reuse of an Indigenous place
relationship_note: small garrison post deliberately sited at the ancient city for protection of the site; exact footprint not documented
flag_detail: Protective deployment against Guatemalan looting and incursions; no destruction, restriction of Indigenous access or litigation documented.

name: Presidio de San Miguel de Horcasitas
location: San Miguel de Horcasitas, Sonora, Mexico
builder: Spanish Crown (Nueva España), founded 1749 under Governor Diego Ortiz Parrilla; moved to Pitic/Hermosillo in the 1780s
beneath: Lands and settlement site of the Seri pueblos of Nuestra Señora del Pópulo and Los Ángeles on the Río San Miguel: a UNAM Estudios de Historia Novohispana study states the presidio was founded on land taken from the Seri pueblos, whose people "fueron los primeros pobladores del paraje que luego ocupó el presidio de San Miguel", and that the lands "pertenecían a dichos naturales". The Seri reductions were Jesuit mission pueblos (c.1700) on Seri ancestral territory; no excavated pre-Columbian site is reported.
relationship: Deliberate reuse of an Indigenous place
relationship_note: presidio placed on the site and lands of Seri mission pueblos; pre-contact occupation of the exact spot not archaeologically documented
flag_detail: Documented dispossession: Seris of Pópulo and Los Ángeles displaced from their lands to make way for the presidio and Spanish settlers (1749), a trigger of the Seri uprising; no litigation or repatriation.

name: Presidio del Norte (Presidio de Nuestra Señora de Belén y Santiago de las Amarillas de la Junta de los Ríos), Ojinaga
location: Ojinaga, Chihuahua, Mexico (La Junta de los Ríos, confluence of the Río Conchos and Río Bravo)
builder: Spanish Crown (Nueva Vizcaya): built 1759–60 by Capt. Manuel Muñoz after Rubín de Celis; moved to Julimes 1767; re-established at La Junta 1773 by Hugo O Connor; Mexican garrison to 1835
beneath: The La Junta de los Ríos village cluster: sedentary farming pueblos of the La Junta phase (from c. AD 1200) seen by Cabeza de Vaca in 1535 and later entradas. The 1760 presidio was built beside the native pueblo of Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe, probably within present-day Ojinaga; the presidio site is believed to lie under the modern town and has not been located archaeologically. Related La Junta village sites (Millington, Polvo) are documented on the Texas bank.
relationship_note: fort sited at the Indigenous village cluster, beside the Guadalupe pueblo; direct superposition unconfirmed
flag_detail: No destruction or litigation documented; the native villages lost their distinct identity by the Mexican period.

name: Escuela Militar de Montaña 'Juan Domingo Perón' (Ejército Argentino training lands, Bariloche) — Lof Millalonco Ranquehue claim
location: San Carlos de Bariloche, Río Negro, Argentina
builder: Argentine Army; lands held by the State/Army since 1937
beneath: Mapuche ancestral territory occupied by the Millalonco Ranquehue families since the late 19th century, 'desde antes de la instalación de las tropas militares'; INAI survey recognised in 2012; no excavated pre-contact site is cited in the litigation
relationship_note: Mapuche territorial claim over Army training ground; occupation documented from the 1880s, not an excavated pre-Columbian site
flags: Land seizure / displacement; Restricted access; Litigation / inquiry
flag_detail: Documented litigation: Feb 2022 federal judge ordered the Army to hand the community title within 60 days; Ministry of Defence appealed (late), Cámara Federal de General Roca rejected it; prosecutor Stornelli obtained a 'no innovar' measure (Nov 2022); Corte Suprema (30 Mar 2023) admitted the Army/prosecutor appeals and froze the transfer. Defence argues the land is essential for the Escuela Militar de Montaña's training. Update: Corte Suprema (c. 27 Jul 2024) annulled the 2022 first-instance order and sent the case back for a new trial because Río Negro province had not been given intervention; the community (c. 180 ha claimed within >3,000 ha the Army administers, which the Army says it uses for mule grazing) remains on the land.

name: Base militar del Cerro El Alguacil (Inarwa) — Batallón de Artillería N° 2 'La Popa' / Décima Brigada Blindada communications base
location: Cerro El Alguacil, Pueblo Bello–Valledupar, Cesar (Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta), Colombia
builder: Colombian Army (Ministerio de Guerra), from 1962; hill deeded to the Ministry by Escritura Pública 104 of 25 Feb 1965; antennas of Policía, RTVC, Telecom added 1980s–1990s
beneath: Inarwa (Inarwa Tama), a sacred hill of the Arhuaco (Iku) people, 'padre de los alimentos', site of pagamento offerings; Incoder certifies it lies inside the Resguardo Arhuaco and the Línea Negra; the Ministry of Defence disputes this. Sacred natural site, not an excavated archaeological site.
relationship: Built directly on a known site
relationship_note: military base and >480 antennas on a named Arhuaco sacred hill; sacred geography rather than excavated remains
flags: Land seizure / displacement; Restricted access; Litigation / inquiry
flag_detail: Documented: Confederación Indígena Tayrona states the Arhuaco were barred from rituals on the hill from 1962 to 2004 and since then need permits; Army guard post and control barrier; complaint cites anti-personnel mines around the hill. Litigation: Corte Constitucional T-005 of 2016 ordered free access for pagamento ceremonies and a consulta previa on the cultural impact of the base and antennas (Consejo de Estado had revoked the lower court's consulta order); the complaint's request to remove base/antennas was not granted in the visible text.

name: Fort Cépérou (Morne Cépérou; Fort Saint-Michel/Fort Louis successors), Cayenne
builder: Compagnie du Cap du Nord (Rouen) under Charles Poncet de Brétigny, 1643 (a Rouen post c.1638 is also claimed); Vauban-style works 1689–1693; French colonial garrison; Portuguese occupation 1809–1817
years: 1643–c.1864 (almost abandoned); ruins and bell tower remain, site handed to the city of Cayenne in 2009
beneath: The hill (Morne Cépérou) was bought by Brétigny from the local Kalina (Galibi/Carib) people and is named after the Kalina chief Cépérou who sold it; the first wooden fort was built on the hill with the settler village below. No excavated pre-contact structure on the hill is documented in the source.
relationship: Deliberate reuse of an Indigenous place
relationship_note: Indigenous-held hill acquired from a named Kalina chief; pre-contact occupation of the summit not archaeologically documented
flag_detail: None documented beyond the 1643 land transfer; bastions destroyed during the Portuguese occupation; remnant pagoda/bell tower classed monument historique, rehabilitated 2016.

name: 6º Pelotão Especial de Fronteira (6º PEF) Uiramutã
location: Uiramutã, Terra Indígena Raposa Serra do Sol, Roraima, Brazil
builder: Brazilian Army (Programa Calha Norte), works from 2000, inaugurated 2 May 2003
beneath: Built in the Makuxi aldeia of Uiramutã (converted into a municipal seat in 1995 without Indigenous consent) inside the Raposa Serra do Sol Indigenous Land; Indigenous territory rather than an excavated pre-contact site
relationship_note: barracks placed in a Makuxi village within a demarcated Indigenous land; no archaeological site named
flags: Land seizure / displacement; Restricted access; Litigation / inquiry
flag_detail: Documented (Baines, FUNAI Revista Estudos e Pesquisas): pelotão implanted from 2000 'sem consultar as lideranças indígenas'; the Army inaugurated the quartel on 2 May 2003 ignoring a pending lawsuit by the Indigenous communities against its construction; 'Operação Uiramutã' staged to coincide with Indigenous celebrations with shows of force and acts of intimidation (as described by the author).

name: Campo de entrenamiento militar Pampa Campanani (also spelled Campapane; Socoroma; Ejército de Chile artillery and mortar training ground)
location: Pampa Campanani, Socoroma, comuna de Putre, Región de Arica y Parinacota, Chile
builder: Chilean Army; fiscal land assigned by Ministerio de Bienes Nacionales (Decreto Exento N° 215 of 5 July 2017) for artillery and mortar training
beneath: Archaeological study cited by the Corte Suprema: inside Pampa Campanani (southern edge of the middle Lluta valley) a rock shelter ('alerón') with human occupation attributable to hunters and herders, 'caminos troperos' forming part of a prehispanic and posthispanic regional traffic route, plus post-Hispanic mining camp ruins; the Consejo de Monumentos Nacionales stated that more archaeological evidence would be recorded as the land is surveyed
relationship_note: recorded pre-Hispanic sites inside the training ground; Aymara community territory
flag_detail: Documented litigation: Comunidad Indígena Aymara Chucuruma filed a recurso de protección against the Ministries of Bienes Nacionales and Defensa; the Corte Suprema (Tercera Sala, July 2018, divided ruling) suspended the effects of the land-assignment decree until measures to protect the archaeological remains found and still to be found are determined and implemented, holding that artillery/mortar training would breach the State's duty of protection. Destruction was threatened, not documented as occurred. Putre mayor Maricel Gutiérrez asked Bienes Nacionales to annul the decree and relocate the exercises, citing other military-related damage in the region (vehicle driven over the Lluta wetland) and asking that Indigenous use and rights over the land be recognised.

name: Base Aérea de Florianópolis (BAFL) — sítio arqueológico Base Aérea I
location: Carianos/Tapera, south of Ilha de Santa Catarina, Florianópolis, Santa Catarina, Brazil
builder: Brazilian Air Force (Força Aérea Brasileira), 20th century
beneath: Sítio Base Aérea I, a late pre-colonial shallow burial site ('sítio raso de sepultamento') with Itararé-tradition ceramics on a recent marine terrace 'em terrenos da Base Aérea de Florianópolis', dated c. 800 ± 70 BP; excavated by Pe. João Alfredo Rohr in 1958, when only c. 10% of the deposit remained after sand quarrying; skeletal series used in violence/trauma studies (Lessa & Scherer 2008)
relationship_note: recorded pre-colonial burial site inside the air base grounds
flag_detail: Documented: by 1958 the bulk of the site had been destroyed by sand extraction ('exploração de areal'); Rohr also recorded that the old road to the Base Aérea was paved with shells taken from nearby sambaquis (oral information, 1950s–60s). Not attributed to deliberate military action. IPHAN process 1129-T-84 press clipping: workers extracting sand on Base Aérea land unearthed prehistoric skulls and burials under a shell layer before Rohr's excavations.

name: Forte de Óbidos (Forte Pauxis, 1697; 19th-century Fortaleza de Óbidos; Quartel General Gurjão, 1907)
location: Óbidos, Pará (narrowest point of the Amazon), Brazil
builder: Portuguese colonial government (Forte Pauxis started 1697 under Manoel da Mota Siqueira / Antônio de Albuquerque Coelho de Carvalho, with Indigenous labour); Brazilian Empire/Republic rebuilt a fort in the 19th century and a Quartel General (Gurjão) inaugurated 1907
beneath: Excavations by Lucena (1994, 1996) in the parapet of the Forte de Óbidos found evidence of pre-colonial occupation in every cut: 'A superfície em que se deu início à instalação do Forte representava o topo de uma sucessão de camadas de ocupação indígena', with terra preta de índio across all excavated areas of the fort and the Indigenous occupation extending well beyond its footprint; the 1697 fort was named for the Pauxis people settled around the military post
relationship: Built directly on a known site
relationship_note: fort built directly on the top of stratified Indigenous occupation layers (terra preta); Pauxis village nearby
flag_detail: Documented: fort construction/levelling fill overlies three Indigenous occupation layers (Lucena 1994 drawing); authors note later official histories ignored these data. No restriction or litigation recorded.

name: Isla Quiriquina naval complex — Escuela de Grumetes 'Alejandro Navarrete Cisterna', Fuerte Quiriquina Sur and coastal batteries Rondizzoni, Miller and Maruri
location: Isla Quiriquina, Bahía de Concepción, Talcahuano, Región del Biobío, Chile
builder: Chilean Navy; island bought by the Chilean State in 1896 and handed to the Navy; fort battery 1898/1908; school buildings from 1910, school installed 1921; coastal batteries 1928
beneath: Per the Navy's own Revista de Marina (2018), the island's 'primer propietario' was the cacique Leochengo, and Agustín de Zárate (1555) described an island in the bay 'dedicada a sus ídolos, donde hay un gran templo', which the author identifies as Quiriquina; Mapuche-Lafkenche sacred island by chronicle rather than by excavation. No archaeological find on the naval grounds is reported in the source.
relationship: Deliberate reuse of an Indigenous place
relationship_note: whole Indigenous-owned/sacred island taken as a naval school and fortress; pre-contact occupation known from chronicles, not from documented excavation
flag_detail: Access to the island is controlled by the Navy (the source notes this has protected its fossil beds from looting); no destruction, litigation or Indigenous claim documented in the source.

name: Escuela de Fuerzas Especiales de Infantería de Marina (Armada Nacional), Barrancón
location: Barrancón, San José del Guaviare, Guaviare, Colombia
builder: Colombian Navy / Ministerio de Defensa; land ('Agua Bonita') awarded to the Ministry by Incora in May 1998, after the Resguardo Jiw de Barrancón had been constituted
beneath: Resguardo Jiw (Guayabero) de Barrancón: the Corte Constitucional found 19 constructions of the naval school (7 permanent: pool, observation tower, lodging, water tank and plant, school, classrooms, two commando tracks) on 6 ha superimposed on the resguardo; Indigenous territory, no excavated pre-contact site cited
relationship_note: naval special-forces school overlapping a titled Jiw resguardo; the Court called it an 'invasión' and 'superposición'
flags: Land seizure / displacement; Restricted access; Litigation / inquiry
flag_detail: Documented: Corte Constitucional (Auto of 3 Aug 2012, follow-up to T-025/2004 on Jiw and Nükak peoples) ordered the Ministry of Defence to return the land and relocate the base within six months, accompanied by Defensoría del Pueblo, Pastoral Social and ACNUR; press reported three Indigenous people injured by unexploded munitions found near the school; the Defence Minister said the government would appeal.

name: Puesto militar / base de comunicaciones del Cerro Berlín (Ejército Nacional), Toribío
builder: Colombian Army (communications antenna post garrisoned by c. 100 soldiers), established before 2012; date of construction not given in sources
beneath: Cerro Berlín, a mountain the Nasa people hold sacred ('para ellos esa montaña es sagrada', Semana 2012) within the Nasa resguardos of northern Cauca; sacred geography and Indigenous territory rather than an excavated pre-contact site
relationship: Built directly on a known site
relationship_note: army post and antenna on a hill sacred to the Nasa; no archaeological excavation cited
flag_detail: Documented: on 17 July 2012 c. 500 members of the Guardia Indígena carried the soldiers off the hill demanding that all armed actors leave Nasa territory; on 18 July 2012 anti-riot police retook the hill with tear gas, leaving one person dead and more than 20 injured; President Santos refused to withdraw troops. No litigation or formal restriction documented.

name: Forte de Santo Antônio de Gurupá (Dutch Fort Mariocai, 1601–1619; Portuguese fort from 1623)
location: Gurupá, Pará (lower Amazon / Xingu mouth), Brazil
builder: Dutch (1601–1619); Portuguese under Pedro Teixeira and Bento Maciel Parente from 1623; Brazilian Army (8ª Região Militar) small garrison still in 1958; passed to the Ministry of Defence in 1963; restored 2014–2018
beneath: Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi (projeto OCA) research classifies the fort locale as 'um complexo arqueológico indígena pré-colonial e pós-colonial'; the fort was 'construída em 1623 por portugueses sobre uma grande aldeia indígena' (DOL/Goeldi complaint, 2020); restoration 2014–2018 ran concurrently with archaeological excavation whose results are displayed in the fort museum
relationship: Built directly on a known site
relationship_note: Portuguese fort built over a large Indigenous village; site classed as a pre-colonial Indigenous archaeological complex
flag_detail: Documented: fort built on top of a large Indigenous village (1623); in Sept 2020 the on-site museum/exhibition was vandalised and looted after being left without surveillance, prompting a Museu Goeldi complaint to the MPF and Iphan. No Indigenous litigation recorded.
